                "Part": 1,
                "Section": "B",
                "SectionName": "Planning, Budgeting, and Forecasting",
                "Topic": "B.008 sales budget sequencing",
                "MicroTopic": "sales budget sequencing",
                "UniqueConceptKey": "B-008-sales-budget-sequencing",
                "LOSTag": "B.2 Budgeting concepts",
                "Difficulty": "Moderate-Easy",
                "ItemType": "MCQ",
                "ItemStyle": "single-select",
                "Stem": "Zephyr is building the annual profit plan. Which response is most appropriate?",
                "Choices": {
                        "A": "Prepare the sales budget early because it drives production, purchasing, labor, overhead, and cash schedules",
                        "B": "Prepare the production budget without considering expected sales",
                        "C": "Prepare the tax return first because it determines units sold",
                        "D": "Prepare the budgeted balance sheet before estimating sales"
                },
                "CorrectChoice": "A",
                "ExplanationCorrect": "The sales budget is typically the starting point of the master budget because it drives most other budgets. Once sales are forecast, the production budget (and therefore materials, labor, and overhead budgets), the selling and administrative expense budget, and ultimately the cash budget and budgeted financial statements can be prepared. Without a sales estimate, there is no basis for determining how much to produce or what resources are needed.",
                "StudyLinks": [
                        {
                                "label": "IMA CMA Learning Outcome Statements, Part 1 Section B",
                                "url": "https://prodcm.imanet.org/-/media/IMA/Files/Home/IMA-Certifications/CMA-Certification/2024-CMA-Learning-Outcome-Statement-Final.ashx"
                        },
                        {
                                "label": "OpenStax Managerial Accounting: Budgeting",
                                "url": "https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/7-introduction"
                        }
                ],
                "SourceDescription": "Original CMA Part 1 exam-style practice. Not real CMA exam content and not copied from official samples.",
                "Part1OnlyFlag": true,
                "ReviewNote": "If missed or marked, review the linked study materials and rework the underlying concept without looking at the answer.",
                "QuestionID": "P1-B-008",
                "CalculationItem": false,

                        "Screened to exclude Part 2-only topics such as CVP, financial ratio analysis, capital budgeting, corporate finance, ERM, and ethics",
                        "Original practice item with unique micro-topic and stem",
                        "Answer key distribution balanced across A/B/C/D",
                        "Distractors written as plausible CMA-style traps"
                ],
                "ExplanationWrongA": "",
                "ExplanationWrongB": "The production budget depends on the sales budget, not vice versa. Production quantities cannot be determined without first knowing how many units need to be sold.",
                "ExplanationWrongC": "The tax return is prepared after the fiscal year ends using historical financial data. It reflects what already happened, not what will happen. The tax return provides no forward-looking information about forecasted unit sales or budgeted production levels. Building the profit plan around a tax return would reverse the logical sequence of budgeting, where forward-looking sales estimates drive all downstream schedules.",
                "ExplanationWrongD": "The budgeted balance sheet is one of the final outputs of the master budget, not the starting point. It is prepared only after the sales budget, operating budgets, cash budget, and budgeted income statement are complete — because each of these schedules feeds into the ending balances for assets, liabilities, and equity. Preparing the balance sheet before estimating sales would require all of those prior schedules to already be resolved, which is circular and impossible.",
